title: Rapid cognitive decline in a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia: a case report
case_prompt: A Caucasian man in his late 60s with a 4-year history of TP53-negative chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) presented with 2 weeks of reduced mobility and confusion and 2 months of subtle memory decline. He had completed six cycles of ofatumumab and chlorambucil 2 months earlier. Comorbidities included fatty liver, gout, and recurrent respiratory infections with hypogammaglobulinaemia. On presentation, his Glasgow Coma Scale was 14/15 due to confusion; initial neurologic examination was normal. Routine blood tests, including full blood count, metabolic profile, thyroid function, and vitamin levels, were unremarkable. Chest radiography and noncontrast CT of the head showed no acute pathology. Microbiological cultures of blood, urine, and stool were negative. A CT scan of neck, thorax, abdomen, and pelvis showed stable splenomegaly and improvement in lymphadenopathy. During admission, he developed worsening cognitive impairment, loss of independence, and right extensor plantar response. Brain MRI demonstrated asymmetric bilateral frontal white-matter hyperintensities on T2-weighted and FLAIR images, no enhancement with contrast, and a thin rim of diffusion restriction at the advancing edge of the lesions.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. PML suspected — “MRI appearances, in conjunction with the clinical syndrome presenting itself, were felt to be highly suggestive of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML).”  
2. Secondary CNS lymphoma considered — “Other differentials, such as secondary central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma … were considered less likely due to an absence of the typical avid enhancement usually seen on MR imaging.”  
3. CNS CLL infiltration considered — “… and CNS CLL infiltration, were considered less likely due to an absence of the typical avid enhancement usually seen on MR imaging.”
